facts.fact_text: In May 2005, after the applicant had been released from detention but while the criminal case against her was still pending, the applicant and two others, Ms I. and Ms B., decided to stage a static demonstration (пикетирование) in front of various public authorities in Moscow, including the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation.
The purpose of the static demonstration planned by the applicant, Ms I. and Ms B. was to protest against the allegedly unlawful actions of public authorities and corruption.

According to the applicant, the demonstration related to persistent difficulties in relation to pending cases involving law enforcement agencies and courts, in particular in the Irkutsk Region, and the failure of the local authorities to deal with their grievances.
On 7 June 2005 at 9.30 a.m., the applicant and her friends Ms I. and Ms B. placed themselves on a pavement separated from the building of the Federal Judges Qualifications Board by a road.
On 7 June 2005, Ms I. and Ms B. unfolded banners/posters containing their message during the demonstration.

The applicant's written statement at the police station stated that she was holding a static demonstration at 9.45 a.m. on 7 June 2005 in conformity with the Public Gatherings Act, as notified to the authorities on 30 May 2005.
On 7 June 2005, the police officer told the applicant and her friends to cease their demonstration and follow him to the police station.
The police officer compelled the applicant and her friends to follow him to the police station.

An arrest record was drawn up at the police station stating that the applicant was brought to the police station at 9.45 a.m. on 7 June 2005 in relation to an administrative offence under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences for the purpose of compiling a record under Article 27.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The police compiled an administrative offence report stating that on 7 June 2005 the applicant held a non-authorised demonstration, thereby committing an administrative offence under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The Justice of the Peace found the applicant guilty of non-compliance with a lawful order by a police officer, an offence under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The Justice of the Peace sentenced the applicant to seven days of detention, to be counted from the moment of her arrest on the morning of 7 June 2005.
On 27 June 2005, the Presnenskiy District Court of Moscow upheld the judgment of 7 June 2005 against the applicant.

Section 7(1) of the Public Gatherings Act (Federal Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004) provided that a person organising a public gathering (except for a meeting or a static demonstration) should notify in writing the competent public authority not earlier than fifteen and not later than ten days before the date of the event.

Section 7(1) of the Public Gatherings Act (Federal Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004) provided that for a static demonstration by several people notification may be made no later than three days before the demonstration.

Section 7(3) of the Public Gatherings Act (Federal Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004) provided that a notification should contain a reference to the aim of the event, the type of the event, the venue(s) and itineraries, the date and time of the event, the expected number of participants, and the full name, contact address and telephone number of the event organiser.

Section 12(1) of the Public Gatherings Act (Federal Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004) provided that the competent public authority should acknowledge in writing receipt of the notification and indicate the date and time of receipt.

Section 12(1) of the Public Gatherings Act (Federal Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004) provided that the competent public authority should inform the event organiser on the same day — in the case of a notification received less than five days before a static demonstration by several people — of any alternative proposal concerning the event venue and/or time.

Under the Public Gatherings Act (Federal Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004), an organiser of a public gathering was obliged to submit a notification of the public event in conformity with the requirements of section 7 of the Act.

Under the Public Gatherings Act (Federal Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004), an organiser of a public gathering was obliged to inform the public authority in writing whether the alternative proposal concerning the event time and/or venue was accepted.

Under the Public Gatherings Act (Federal Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004), an organiser of a public gathering was obliged to suspend the event or end it if the event participants committed unlawful actions.

Section 5 of the Public Gatherings Act (Federal Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004) provided that the organiser of the event is not allowed to proceed with it if the notification was not submitted in conformity with the time-limit or if the authority's alternative proposal for another venue and/or time for the event was not settled with the public authority.
Under the Public Gatherings Act (Federal Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004), a public event could be held in any suitable venue.
Section 8 of the Public Gatherings Act (Federal Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004) provided that no public event could be held in the immediate vicinity of court buildings.

Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided that non-compliance with a lawful order by a police officer, given within the scope of his or her professional duties, is punishable by a fine or administrative detention of up to fifteen days.

Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided that violation of the rules or procedure for organising or participating in a public gathering (a meeting, demonstration or static demonstration) is punishable by a fine.

The Justice of the Peace established that on 7 June 2005 the applicant failed to comply with a lawful order by police officers and failed to end a non-authorised demonstration in front of the Supreme Court of Russia.

The Justice of the Peace found that the police officers' order to the applicant and her companions to accompany them to the police station was lawful and justified, also in view of the defendants' refusals to show identity documents.

The Presnenskiy District Court of Moscow found on 27 June 2005 that on 7 June 2005 the applicant held a non-authorised demonstration and held a banner containing a very negative assessment of the professional activity of the Prosecutor General, the President of the Supreme Court and the Minister of Justice.

The Presnenskiy District Court of Moscow found on 27 June 2005 that the applicant refused to comply with lawful orders to end the violation of the public order and threatened police officers with prosecution, thereby resisting a lawful order by police officers.
On 30 May 2005, the applicant, Ms I. and Ms B. sent a telegram to the Moscow Mayor's Office informing the authorities of their intention to stage static demonstrations between 3 and 16 June 2005.
On 31 May 2005, the Moscow Mayor's Office acknowledged receipt of the telegram sent by the applicant, Ms I. and Ms B. on 30 May 2005.
At 9.45 a.m. on 7 June 2005, the applicant and her friends were approached by several police officers, one of whom asked them to show documents justifying their demonstration.

The applicant explained to the police officer that they needed no authorisation and produced the telegram message sent to the Moscow Mayor's Office and the certified copy of the telegram bearing the mayor's office stamp.
The applicant and her friends refused to comply with the police officer's order to cease their demonstration and follow him to the police station.
While in the police station on 7 June 2005, the applicant made a written statement indicating that she came to Moscow to protect her rights against various law enforcement agencies.

The applicant's written statement at the police station stated that she was holding a static demonstration at 9.45 a.m. on 7 June 2005 in conformity with the Public Gatherings Act, as notified to the authorities on 30 May 2005.
The applicant's written statement at the police station stated that she was arrested by a person wearing a police uniform who refused to introduce himself and to show his licence.

The applicant's written statement at the police station stated that the officers told her that their superior had ordered that the demonstrators be taken to the police station without explaining the actual reasons for the arrest.
The applicant's written statement at the police station stated that under section 18 of the Public Gatherings Act the police should not impede the exercise of the right to freedom of assembly.
The applicant's written statement at the police station stated that there were no reasons to stop and disperse the demonstration under section 15 of the Public Gatherings Act.
The police decided that the applicant and her friends should be brought before the Justice of the Peace in the 375th Circuit of the Arbatskiy District of Moscow.
The examination of the applicant's case before the Justice of the Peace started at or around 10 p.m. on 7 June 2005 and lasted some minutes.
The applicant unsuccessfully sought an adjournment before the Justice of the Peace to have time to study the case file and to prepare her defence.

The Justice of the Peace established that on 7 June 2005 the applicant failed to comply with a lawful order by police officers and failed to end a non-authorised demonstration in front of the Supreme Court of Russia.

The Justice of the Peace dismissed the applicant's request to obtain external video recordings of the building of the Supreme Court of Russia, finding no reason to doubt the veracity of the administrative offence record.

Police officer Mr S. was heard as a witness before the Justice of the Peace and stated that he and his colleagues asked the demonstration participants to show documents relating to the authorisation of the public event.

Police officer Mr S. stated that the applicant handed over a telegram and that since there were doubts as to the authenticity of the document, the applicant and the other two were asked to show their identity documents.

Police officer Mr S. stated that since the applicant and the other two refused to show identity documents despite several warnings, the police took them to the police station to determine their identities and to determine the circumstances relating to the lawfulness of the demonstration.
Police officer Mr S. stated that since the applicant and the others refused to follow the police, they were compelled to do so.
The Justice of the Peace found that the documents produced by the applicant had been amended and that the police officers had sufficient reasons to doubt their authenticity.

The Justice of the Peace found that the police officers' order to the applicant and her companions to accompany them to the police station was lawful and justified, also in view of the defendants' refusals to show identity documents.
The applicant was released on 14 June 2005, having served the sentence imposed by the Justice of the Peace.

The Presnenskiy District Court of Moscow found on 27 June 2005 that on 7 June 2005 the applicant held a non-authorised demonstration and held a banner containing a very negative assessment of the professional activity of the Prosecutor General, the President of the Supreme Court and the Minister of Justice.

The Presnenskiy District Court of Moscow found on 27 June 2005 that the applicant refused to comply with lawful orders to end the violation of the public order and threatened police officers with prosecution, thereby resisting a lawful order by police officers.
The Presnenskiy District Court of Moscow noted on 27 June 2005 that section 8 of the Public Gatherings Act prohibits public events in the immediate vicinity of court buildings.
On 1 July 2005, the Presnenskiy District Court of Moscow examined Ms I.'s appeal and discontinued the administrative offence case against her.

The Presnenskiy District Court of Moscow found on 1 July 2005 that the administrative proceedings against Ms I. were initiated in relation to a fact falling within the scope of Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences rather than Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The Presnenskiy District Court of Moscow found on 1 July 2005 that sufficient evidence was not adduced at first instance to find Ms I. guilty of the offence under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
On 6 July 2005, the Presnenskiy District Court of Moscow quashed the first-instance judgment in respect of Ms B. and discontinued the administrative offence case against her.

The Presnenskiy District Court of Moscow found on 6 July 2005 that the administrative offence record against Ms B. referred to unlawful demonstrating falling within the scope of Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The Presnenskiy District Court of Moscow found on 6 July 2005 that sufficient evidence was not adduced at first instance to find Ms B. guilty of the offence under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
